name: Mariner 4
objective: First successful flyby of Mars; return close-up images of the Martian surface.
description: Mariner 4 performed the first successful Mars flyby on 14–15 July 1965, returning 22 close-up images of the cratered Martian surface. These images revealed a moon-like, heavily cratered landscape and showed Mars had a thin CO₂ atmosphere. It fundamentally changed scientific understanding of Mars.

name: Mariner 6
objective: Flyby of Mars to study surface and atmosphere; support planning for future lander missions.
description: Mariner 6 flew past Mars on 31 July 1969, returning 75 far-encounter and close-encounter images. It studied the Martian atmosphere and surface, covering the equatorial region.

name: Mariner 7
objective: Flyby of Mars to study surface and atmosphere; cover southern regions including polar cap.
description: Mariner 7 flew past Mars on 5 August 1969, returning 126 images. It covered the southern hemisphere and polar cap, complementing Mariner 6's equatorial observations.

name: Mariner 8
objective: Planned Mars orbiter to map 70% of the Martian surface and monitor weather.
description: Mariner 8 failed to reach orbit when its Atlas-Centaur launch vehicle malfunctioned. It fell into the Atlantic Ocean shortly after launch on 8 May 1971.

name: Mariner 9
objective: First spacecraft to orbit Mars; map the entire Martian surface; study atmosphere and moons Phobos and Deimos.
description: Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet when it entered Mars orbit on 14 November 1971. It mapped 85% of the Martian surface and revealed Olympus Mons (the largest volcano in the solar system), Valles Marineris, and evidence of ancient riverbeds. The mission ended when attitude control gas was depleted on 27 October 1972.

name: Viking 1 Orbiter
objective: Provide high-resolution mapping, serve as relay for Viking 1 Lander, and study Mars atmosphere.
description: Viking 1 Orbiter entered Mars orbit on 19 June 1976 and operated until attitude control fuel was depleted on 7 August 1980. It returned over 50,000 images and served as the primary communication relay for the Viking 1 Lander.

name: Viking 2 Orbiter
objective: High-resolution mapping, communication relay for Viking 2 Lander, atmospheric science.
description: Viking 2 Orbiter entered Mars orbit on 7 August 1976 and operated until attitude control fuel was depleted on 25 July 1978. It returned valuable data on Mars' north polar region.

name: Mars Observer
objective: Global mapping of Martian surface morphology, topography, composition, gravity, and magnetic field.
description: Mars Observer was lost on 21 August 1993, just three days before its planned Mars orbit insertion. Contact was permanently lost, likely due to a rupture in the fuel pressurisation line. It was the USA's first Mars mission in 17 years.

name: Mars Global Surveyor
objective: Global mapping of Mars surface, topography, gravity, magnetic field, and atmospheric monitoring.
description: Mars Global Surveyor entered Mars orbit on 12 September 1997 and conducted aerobraking to reach its mapping orbit. It operated for over nine years, providing comprehensive maps of Mars including the MOLA topography dataset. Contact was lost on 2 November 2006, likely due to a battery failure.

name: Mars Climate Orbiter
objective: Study Martian climate, atmosphere, and surface changes over a full Martian year.
description: Mars Climate Orbiter was lost on 23 September 1999 when it entered the atmosphere at too low an altitude due to a navigation error caused by a units mismatch (metric vs imperial). This became a landmark case study in the importance of engineering standards.

name: Mars Odyssey
objective: Map the chemical and mineralogical composition of Mars; detect water and shallow buried ice.
description: Mars Odyssey entered Mars orbit on 24 October 2001 and is the longest-operating Mars spacecraft in history, still operational as of 2026. It discovered vast deposits of hydrogen (indicating water ice) in the polar regions and has served as a critical communications relay for surface missions including Curiosity and Perseverance.

name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
objective: Detailed reconnaissance and climate study of Mars; search for landing sites for future missions.
description: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) entered Mars orbit on 10 March 2006 and carries the most powerful camera ever sent to another planet — HiRISE. It has returned more data than all other Mars missions combined and continues to operate as of 2026, serving as a key communication relay for surface assets.

name: MAVEN
objective: Investigate how Mars lost its atmosphere and liquid water over time by studying solar wind interaction.
description: MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN) entered Mars orbit on 22 September 2014. It has shown that solar wind stripped Mars of most of its atmosphere billions of years ago. MAVEN also serves as a communications relay and continues to operate as of 2026.

name: Mars Orbiter Mission — Mangalyaan
objective: Demonstrate ISRO's capability to design, plan, and execute an interplanetary mission; study Martian surface, atmosphere, and exosphere.
description: Mangalyaan (Hindi for 'Mars-craft') was India's first interplanetary mission and Asia's first successful Mars mission. It was developed in 15 months. It successfully entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 — India became the fourth space agency and first Asian country to achieve Mars orbit on its first attempt. The spacecraft was declared lost on 2 October 2022 after losing contact, likely due to battery depletion following a long eclipse. It carried five scientific instruments studying Martian surface morphology, mineralogy, and exospheric deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio.

mangalyaanFacts.significance: India's first interplanetary mission; first Asian country to reach Mars orbit; first to do so on its maiden attempt

name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
objective: Demonstrate powered, controlled flight on another planet; scout terrain for Perseverance rover.
description: Ingenuity was a technology demonstration helicopter that flew with Perseverance. It made humanity's first powered flight on another planet on 19 April 2021. It exceeded expectations, completing 72 flights before rotor damage from a hard landing on 18 January 2024 ended the mission. As a secondary payload, it is tracked here as part of the Mars 2020 mission group.

name: Mariner 3
objective: Attempt a Mars flyby and conduct interplanetary science observations.
description: The payload shroud failed to separate, and the spacecraft lost power before it could enter a proper Mars-transfer trajectory. It never reached Mars.

name: Mars Cube One (MarCO-A and MarCO-B)
objective: Demonstrate interplanetary CubeSats and relay InSight entry, descent, and landing data to Earth.
description: The twin CubeSats flew past Mars during InSight’s landing and relayed its telemetry in near real time. MarCO-B also returned an image of Mars during the flyby.

name: ESCAPADE (Twin Mars Orbiters)
objective: Study how the solar wind interacts with Mars’ magnetosphere and contributes to atmospheric escape.
description: NASA’s twin spacecraft launched on 13 November 2025 and are en route to Mars. NASA currently plans Mars orbit insertion in September 2027.
